summary:
Traces on the Celestial Dust: Project Summary

This project, presented by Rhodes Park School Group 2, tells the story of the equipment NASA left behind on Luna (the Moon) and Mars after their missions ended. These machines are abandoned but not forgotten. Each one is a silent monument that still tells us how we explore.

On the Moon, Surveyor landers proved that soft landings were possible. Apollo’s descent stages, three moon buggies and the ALSEP science packages stayed behind when the astronauts left. On Mars, the Viking landers and the Sojourner rover were the first machines to touch down and roam the surface. Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix and InSight later worked far beyond their planned lifespans. Ingenuity made the first powered flight on another world before it was grounded.

Together, these artifacts show the achievements of space exploration. Their details come from NASA’s Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA).
details:
What does it do or how does it work?
Traces on the Celestial Dust is a seven-slide animated presentation about the equipment NASA left behind on the Moon and Mars. It defines the topic first, then moves through the lunar hardware (Surveyor landers, Apollo modules, moon buggies, ALSEP science packages) and the Martian machines (Viking, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight, Ingenuity). Each slide pairs a short explanation with a matching space image. Images and text cards animate in automatically, and each slide has its own transition. Speaker notes are included for the presenter.

What benefits does it have?

  • It makes space history easy for a school audience to follow.
  • It focuses on one clear message per slide, with short text and relevant images.
  • The speaker notes let any team member present confidently.
  • It corrects an error in the first draft (the Viking landers arrived in 1976, not 1973).

What is the intended impact?
To help students and teachers see that space exploration leaves a lasting legacy. We want the audience to value the machines that came before and to feel curious about the history and science of exploring the Moon and Mars.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Our original slides were made in a Google Slides/PowerPoint format and provided the starting content and images.
  • The new deck was built with an AI assistant (Claude by Anthropic), which generated the presentation file using JavaScript (Node.js with the pptxgenjs library).
  • A Python script added the slide transitions and entrance animations to the file’s XML.
  • The deck was checked with a file validator and rendered through LibreOffice for visual review, and it opens in Microsoft PowerPoint.
  • The images came from the original presentation, and the background facts reference NASA’s NSSDCA archive.

If your competition requires you to declare AI assistance, mention it in your own words so your submission is accurate.

How is your project creative?

  • It uses a space-inspired dark theme with Mars-orange, gold and NASA-blue accents.
  • The title, “Traces on the Celestial Dust,” turns equipment left on the Moon and Mars into a story about the marks humans leave on other worlds.
  • It treats each abandoned machine as a “silent monument.”
  • Varied animations and transitions give the slides a sense of motion and discovery.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Audience: a school audience that needs clear, short explanations.
  • Accuracy: facts and dates were checked and corrected, and sources point to NASA.
  • Visual relevance: every image was chosen to match its slide, and the unrelated cartoon images were removed.
  • Length and flow: the deck was kept to seven slides, starting with a definition of the topic.
  • Readability: the text is large enough to read, with strong contrast and consistent layouts.
  • Presenting: speaker notes and automatic animations make it easy to deliver.
